A crucial factor in determining this spacing involves analyzing the visibility areas between nearby bases, a task made complex by varying user locations and equipment configurations. This study aims to investigate how changes in user positions and antenna settings affect the non-intersecting visibility areas in MIMO bases, with results showing that area variability can be substantial, with up to 5 times difference. Furthermore, as the stochastic access protocol becomes more aggressive, these areas tend to converge, reducing spacing requirements. With this in mind, researchers suggest setting a minimum spacing based on the average area, rather than a fixed value.

Recent observations at sub-millimeter/millimeter wavelengths have revealed that the morphological structure of young stars' surrounding disks comprise various shapes, including symmetrical patterns and features resembling spiral arms, and localized curved formations. Prior research primarily focused on modeling planetary interactions to explain observed patterns in disks. Although some exoplanets have been identified in such systems, many of these substructures emerge even before planetary formation as necessary precursors that lead to material redistribution, the creation of complex patterns and ultimately, cache small solid particles that deliver essential raw material for planet formation. This work employs high-resolution, three-dimensional radiative hydrodynamic simulations in conjunction with radiative transfer modeling to predict the appearance of disks undergoing vertical shear instability (VSI) at a range of wavelengths from the near-infrared to a few mm. It shows that VSI leads to material rearrangement, resulting in the formation of localized curved formations, bridging the gap between linear perturbation analysis and comprehensive simulations. Furthermore, it highlights that the spectral energy distribution of stars surrounded by VSI-driven substructures exhibits a marginal increase compared to those without such structures.

The New York group's new finite-range antisymmetrization (FRS) technique yields an all-encompassing energy expression that incorporates a central, peripheral antisymmetrization component and is analogous to the Hartree-Fock method. By leveraging the success of the FRS approach for nucleon-scattering data analysis, researchers can now apply this method to investigate the properties of finite nuclei and celestial objects by utilizing the energy density functional (EDF) framework in conjunction with finite-range interactions. A new interaction called the "Big Apple" was developed to describe infinite and finite nuclei, as well as celestial objects, by incorporating a specific type of two-body tensor interaction. Consequently, this interaction yields an improved description of exotic quantum phenomena observed in nuclei, and the FRS method allows it to be connected directly to the microscopic components of finite nuclei and celestial objects.

This research focuses on creating frequency-independent Molmer-Sorensen gates for ion-trap quantum computing, enabling successful implementation of two-qubit phase rotations and providing a key component for universal quantum gate sets. Given the inherent challenge of accurately aligning multiple motional modes' frequencies, we develop a frequency-resilient gate technique that leverages balanced input light across all modes. As a result, a demonstration of large-scale (up to 20) collective motion remains frequency-independent, utilizing only a limited range of light intensity. Furthermore, frequency domains associated with both the 264Hz global oscillation and the 264Hz shift of the 13th motional mode have been successfully manipulated with just a 1.5 times increase in light intensity above the threshold, confirming the practicality of this approach for real-world applications.

Recently, a new class of materials called strongly coupled Dirac metals has been introduced, characterized by coupled electron and hole Dirac cones at the Fermi level. These materials exhibit unusual electronic properties, including gapless behavior and magnetic field-induced topological phase transitions. A naturally occurring alloy, Gd(Tc,N) with a tetragonal crystal structure, is predicted to be a strongly linked Dirac metal. This predicted material features a unique arrangement of coupled electron and hole Dirac cones around the $\Gamma$ point in its band structure, and theoretical calculations indicate it should exhibit unusual magnetic properties, including zero-field strong anisotropy of the resistivity and specific heat, and magnetic field-induced polarization reversal and topological phase transitions.

The NA62 experiment at CERN's 18 GeV proton beam facility can accurately detect rare decay events of charged particles. A key focus of the NA62 research is on identifying neutral lepton contributions that could explain observed anomalies in the (muon) sector. Although initially designed to study muon decay, the NA62 detector can also be highly sensitive to rare electron decays, allowing it to investigate a specific neutral lepton scenario where a neutrally charged dark matter particle is produced in the decay of charged kaons. Specifically, NA62 can examine the $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ decay pattern for signs of a particular neutral lepton with a mass of 200 MeV, which would result in an excess of 0.05 events per milliradian per luminosity unit. Nevertheless, NA62's current limitations mean it cannot accurately measure the neutrino's scattering width off the Standard Model particles.

The limitations of large language models have been highlighted in recent studies, showcasing situations where neural models fall behind traditional $N$-gram methods. To address this, our research aims to reintroduce the benefits of $N$-gram models while leveraging the strengths of neural models. We achieve this by incorporating a novel residual learning framework that allows neural models to focus on complex, high-frequency data patterns. In return, the neural network is able to learn a simplified, low-frequency $n$-gram model components, effectively relearning fundamental language knowledge. Through extensive experiments on language modeling and machine translation tasks, our findings consistently show that this hybrid approach outperforms the standalone neural model, with a particular boost in sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores.

Reconstructing accurate three-dimensional faces from single images or internet sources is a difficult task due to variations in pose, expressions, and data quality. To address this challenge, we present a robust facial reconstruction framework called SADRNet, which leverages both the current image and additional photos of the individual. The proposed architecture consists of two primary components: a facial regression network and a refinement network. The regression network produces an intermediate three-dimensional face mesh, which is then further processed by the refinement network using both the input image and additional photos. We implement a self-alignment mechanism to correct the 3D face mesh based on the features extracted from the photos. The framework is evaluated on the widely used Florence 3D Face Reconstruction Dataset and achieves state-of-the-art performance in both metrics, outperforming existing methods with additional photos. The code is available online.

In the early universe, a specific type of cosmic inflation known as $\alpha$-attractor inflation led to the formation of black hole precursors, which in turn became primordial black holes (PBHs). Researchers have challenged this theory by claiming that the initial perturbations required for PBH formation could arise from the analysis of cosmic microwave background anisotropies and therefore may not need additional assumptions. This paper disputes this idea by arguing that the perturbations driving PBH formation must comply with specific criteria outlined in the $\alpha$-attractor inflation model, which include a particular frequency range and amplitude. Consequently, the authors demonstrate that the perturbations generating PBHs fall outside the CMB multipoles and cannot be accounted for by CMB anomalies, thereby supporting the initial assumption that PBH formation results from secondary gravitational perturbations rather than CMB initial perturbations.

Researchers examined labeled ordered trees with the ability to impose a left-to-right order on their vertices, using this order to assign labels to the trees' vertices. Focus was placed on identifying the most deeply labeled vertices in these trees, defining the term "deepest" to mean the farthest from the trees' root while still being equidistant from leaves. Additional notation was introduced to represent the number of leaves within the most deeply labeled subtree of a given tree, denoted as the deepest leaf label (DLL). Investigations explored patterns of DLL values across various tree classes, enabling proofs of established conjectures and suggesting avenues for further research.

This research focuses on an issue encountered during the 2020 US presidential election recount in Georgia, where a manual re-count of hand-marked paper ballots led to discrepancies found by the state's voting system. To address this challenge, an innovative approach called Informed Optical Character Recognition (iOCR) was developed to accurately count ballot marks. iOCR utilizes a unique two-stage approach where an initial character recognition process is followed by a machine learning-based verification step to address uncertainties and boost accuracy. Experiments conducted on real data showed that iOCR outperforms the existing GeorgiaSmartballots OCR system in terms of accuracy, with a 99.99% correction rate for simple ballots and a 97.5% rate for more complex ones.

In recent years, over-parameterization has been successfully applied to linear regression and neural networks, enabling the direct solution of linear systems without iterative optimization. This approach has been extended to time series models by Li, et al. who presented an approach to solve linear dynamics models with over-parameterization, resulting in the SPAN model. Building upon this work, we show that over-parameterization can be combined with time series models in a non-linear framework through the inclusion of state-dependent nonlinear functions, enabling direct solution of the parameters. We validate this approach, referred to as Benign Misfitting, on synthetic and real-world data sets, achieving performance comparable to conventional neural network-based methods.

A key challenge in current energy management models lies in adequately addressing uncertainty, especially in relation to consumer electricity demand. This research focuses on developing a robust decision-making framework to handle this uncertainty in a multi-agent, decentralized market structure. A novel, risk-averse storage self-planning approach is introduced, prioritizing the mitigation of adverse effects from negative price shocks and unanticipated demand increases. This method employs a new risk measure that considers both expected losses and the severity of extreme events. Unlike conventional risk-neutral optimization, this approach avoids the normality assumption for future demand distributions. As such, it maintains flexibility in modeling future demand patterns. The proposed method is demonstrated to enhance social welfare through simulated tests in a day-ahead market with multiple agents.

A simplified computer model is used to explore how atmospheric circulation changes in response to various rotation speeds and temperature differences between the equator and poles in a planet's atmosphere. This analysis is compared across six different test cases with vastly different circulation modes, ranging from extremely fast "super-rotation" to slow "turbulence". Despite these diverse scenarios, a consistent pattern of atmospheric circulation emerges, revealing that atmospheric movement follows a specific and predictable path defined by its physical parameters. Furthermore, reducing complexity in the model's initial conditions does not noticeably alter the predicted pattern of circulation. These findings are particularly relevant for understanding atmospheric circulation on planets with slow rotation speeds, such as gas giants, where atmospheric movement is influenced by factors like wind speed and temperature gradients.

Deep neural networks have achieved superior performance in various computer vision tasks.
Due to the enormous size of the ImageNet dataset, standard data augmentation techniques,
such as random cropping and color jittering, are widely applied to prevent overfitting.
However, the positive effect of these techniques diminishes as the network depth increases,
and, in turn, a simpler data augmentation strategy might be more efficient.
In this study, a novel learning approach called Dynamic ImageNet is proposed,
where the data augmentation strategy adapts in accordance with the network's learning phase.
Specifically, more intensive data augmentation is employed during the initial training phase,
and this intensity gradually decreases as the network enters the later training stages.
To enhance the adaptability further, a magnitude-based learning rate adjustment is introduced,
where the learning rate changes in proportion to the network's depth,
and this results in improved performance on CIFAR-100 and SVHN.
Furthermore, the proposed method yields comparable results to the state-of-the-art performance
obtained with deep residual networks on the ImageNet dataset.

Researchers who utilize silicon surface code exchange-linked donor pairs for quantum computing need to understand how donor electrons behave under stress. Accurate simulations of donor electron behavior require accounting for the interactions between silicon's electronic valleys and its response to stress. This paper presents a novel approach, incorporating a new multi-valley effective weight method, which accurately describes the weight of electronic weight within valley spaces even in situations with significant valley mixing. This approach is demonstrated to accurately simulate stress-induced changes in donor electron behavior using a comprehensive method that accounts for valley interactions and static and zero-point lattice fluctuations. This model's results are compared to alternative methods and experimental data, showing that the multi-valley effective weight approach provides a clear and stress-induced explanation for donor electron behavior.

Our investigation focused on HgTe quantum trenches, which exhibit a unique Te-Hg-Te crystal structure and feature extremely narrow band gaps, allowing for the realization of gapless quantum states. Utilizing highly sensitive magnetic resonance imaging, we detected localized states within the trenches and confirmed their extension into the Kramers-Kronig relations-derived gapless region. Furthermore, we observed the excitation of surface plasmons in the long wavelength limit and found that the lack of a energy gap results in surface plamon excitation being detectable throughout the trenches, regardless of their width. This indicates that tunneling of Dirac particles can occur freely, indicating quantum transport properties that exhibit both one-dimensional and two-dimensional behavior simultaneously.

In Time-Division Duplexing (TDD) networks, model allocation refers to assigning different scheduling models to various components of a base station. This allows base stations to adapt to changing traffic requirements and improve overall performance. However, as the number of base stations increases, managing model allocation becomes a complex challenge. Existing static allocation approaches fail to keep up with the dynamic nature of TDD networks. This paper presents a dynamic allocation framework, utilizing a non-cooperative game theory paradigm. This framework enables a centralized controller to efficiently manage model allocation across the network, even in large-scale scenarios. The proposed approach ensures optimal allocation according to various performance optimization objectives, while considering the unpredictable arrival and departure of base stations. The effectiveness of this allocation strategy is proven through numerical results, demonstrating substantial improvements in key performance indicators (KPIs) such as throughput, delay, and model diversity.

In this work, we examine whether Neural Networks can be trained using Hamiltonian Dynamics. If this is possible, it would significantly enhance the stability and performance of large Neural Networks through the application of more efficient optimizers. To investigate this concept, we developed a simple Hamiltonian Neural Network training framework. However, our primary discovery is that standard Neural Networks cannot be trained using standard Hamiltonian optimizers. In particular, we found that the Hamiltonian Neural Network's Hamiltonian dynamics leads to divergent gradients in traditional Neural Networks. To overcome this challenge, we present a novel Hamiltonian Neural Network architecture that can train standard Neural Networks using Hamiltonian dynamics. Our experiments show that this method outperforms traditional optimizers on a range of tasks including Hamiltonian Chaos, additive noise reduction, Hamiltonian denoising autoencoders, and stochastic Hamiltonian autoencoders.

Artificial neural networks and machine learning models can be unreliable due to biases in their training data or complex patterns in new data. This paper presents a novel hybrid method that combines the outcomes of these models with human feedback in real-time, aiming to increase their dependability. The method involves two primary components: a simple yet effective trust rating system for models and a data enhancement technique. During each batch processing cycle, the trust rating system assesses the reliability of the model output based on its consistency with human input, assigning a confidence value to each data point. This value is then utilized to remove unreliable data points from further analysis. The data enrichment technique involves creating fake data entries by manipulating model output and incorporating them into the model's training data. This approach prevents the model from overfitting on the fake data. This hybrid method is tested on real-world data and compared to alternative methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving model reliability.

This paper introduces a distinguished class of quantum invariant polynomials in the Kauffman polynomial regime, specifically for links in the product of the torus $T^2$ and the interval $I$. A key characteristic of these invariants is their potential implication on the volume hypothesis, a long-standing conjectural scenario that connects the geometric properties of hyperbolic 3-manifolds to their combinatorial representations through invariants derived from quantum topology. The volume hypothesis is marked by two key features: firstly, a polynomial growth rate in relation to the volume, and secondly, distinct coefficients for 1- and 2-cusped manifolds. The introduced invariants exhibit both of these properties, demonstrating polynomial scaling with volume and displaying a distinction between 1- and 2-cusped manifolds, including examples of the latter where the coefficient vanishes. These invariants can be computed for an extensive range of volume-preserving deformations, including gluing, splitting, and merging of torus-boundary components, as well as rearrangements of link complements within the same manifolding space. The term "volume hypothesis behavior" is used here to describe invariants that exhibit these characteristics, capturing both the polynomial volume scaling and the differential marking of 1- and 2-cusped manifolds. Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) aims to accurately determine the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context. Deep neural networks, particularly BERT-based models, have achieved significant progress in this area, thanks in part to the incorporation of word context. However, since the context provided in standard WSD datasets often suffices, additional information provided in the Context Gloss Enhancement (CGE) task tends to be superfluous or even misleading. As such, a straightforward approach that leverages a single BERT-based model has been shown to yield comparable performance to more complex models, thereby serving as a benchmark for comparison. Furthermore, a head-only network architecture has been explored, which has been found to integrate additional context effectively, thereby providing insights into the limited benefits of extra context in WSD.

The reciprocal Gamma function plays a key role in establishing conformal mappings, particularly in problems involving mixed Neumann boundary conditions. However, evaluating its potential uses is complicated by the limited availability of efficient numerical methods to calculate it. To address this challenge, we present a series of developments aimed at making the reciprocal Gamma function more practical for applications. Initially, we create an original integral representation of the reciprocal Gamma function, followed by the derivation of several new formulations, including their dual versions. Notably, these formulations enable the derivation of explicit reciprocoses for the traditional Gamma function, offering alternative proofs of known formulas.

Based on an analogy with proton-proton interactions, it is proposed to identify the location of the top quark production region in proton-nucleus collisions by detecting the charge of the slowest-moving charged particle in high-multiplicity events. Specifically, it is suggested that events featuring three hadrons with transverse momenta over 2 GeV, situated within a pseudorapidity interval of 1 unit, be analyzed to pinpoint the top quark's generation. Assuming that 10 events per second meet this criterion in high-energy lead-proton collisions, it is estimated that approximately 1 out of 10 events will exhibit the characteristics of top quark production, thereby extending the search for rare processes beyond the current limits in proton-nucleus interactions.

Understanding and generating code for databases is a complex task that involves natural language processing, stochastic computation, and optimization. Current approaches divide the process into two steps, separating natural language understanding from database generation. However, research has shown that certain models, specifically LLMs, can perform the combined task successfully. Inspired by this finding, we propose a novel method that utilizes a mixed parameter LLM to perform cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing. This model incorporates two supportive tasks to facilitate LLM parameter sharing, enabling the model to produce accurate SQL queries given natural language inputs across various domains. Evaluations using the Spider dataset reveal that our approach surpasses the performance of separate natural language understanding and generation components, also surpassing the current state-of-the-art in the field.

The underlying structure of numerous high-value datasets can be effectively represented as graph-based models, offering a more intuitive understanding and streamlined processing capabilities. As a result, graph-based storage and processing frameworks have gained widespread popularity across various applications and platforms. However, enhancing security controls while maintaining efficiency and performance in graph-based data systems has proven challenging, especially when imposing strict confidentiality constraints and achieving scalable performance. Current solutions often prioritize integrity over confidentiality or compromise on performance, neglecting the middle ground where confidentiality and efficiency coexist. In the endeavor to rectify this shortcoming, we examine existing approaches to confidentiality controls within graph-based data systems, exploring notable applications, pioneering techniques, and cutting-edge research, before delving into the underlying challenges and potential future directions.

The vast amount of images and data Euclid will produce holds significant value for
heritage science purposes. With an estimated 65 terabytes of data, Euclid will exceed
the resources of a single institution, necessitating a collaborative effort among
a broad community of researchers and institutions. To meet this challenge, a plan
is in place to provide open access to raw and processed data and images via the
European Space Agency's Data and Service Hub. This approach enables users to
directly access and manipulate the data without reliance on intermediate products,
facilitating more efficient use of observations. Furthermore, the Euclid Consortium
will provide comprehensive documentation, software tools, and sample analyses to
assist users in leveraging the data effectively. With an anticipated operational
period of nearly 6.25 years and nearly 170 million visited sky positions, Euclid will
generate an enormous legacy for the scientific community, with opportunities for
research across a broad spectrum of astronomical disciplines.

Researchers have been using hydrodynamic theories to understand the dynamics of Bose-Einstein condensates, as the equations mirror those of classical fluids and allow for efficient numerical simulations. However, these theories have limitations when it comes to interacting systems and full phase-space implementations. Diceno and Rota develop a comprehensive framework for interacting Bose gases in one-dimensional case, incorporating a new method for solving the Wigner transform of Gross-Pitaevskii equations, and derive the collisional term of the Vlasov equation from first principles. Additionally, they present two distinct approaches for determining the condensate density, utilizing either the hydrodynamic density or the Wigner function. When applied to a model of a 1D Bose gas with cubic interaction, their predictions demonstrate excellent agreement with quantum simulations.

This research paper introduces a new concept called the homotopy region minimizing surface (RMS) within the framework of metric spaces, specifically for applying to surfaces that map from a disk to a metric space while meeting certain minimization requirements. A key finding shows that when the target metric space allows for sufficient inductive construction of surfaces via 1-parameter families, then surface RMS's can be obtained from surface S0 RMS's through a process of extension. Additionally, for the case of surfaces that map from a 2-dimensional disk, a connection is established between the RMS's and the homotopy class minimizing surfaces, thereby leading to the term "homotopy region minimizing surfaces".

Recent studies indicate that the interaction between the proton and the 64Ni nucleus, specifically regarding monopole interactions, exhibit unique characteristics that differ from other nuclei. Notably, researchers have found that the proton's interaction with 64Ni demonstrates a coexistence of different forms of the nuclear interaction, a phenomenon previously observed only in 1n and 3n knockout reactions using 58Ni and 60Ni nuclei. To further explore this phenomenon, researchers used a 12 GeV electron beam to study the scattering of protons from 64Ni by measuring the asymmetry of the angular distribution of protons scattered by 64Ni. The results showed that the proton's interaction with 64Ni exhibits coexistence form structure, particularly evident in the long-wavelength region. This phenomenon is also observed at zero spin transfer, a first in nuclear physics research. The findings are also consistent with the predictions of the tensor monopole interaction.

Evaluating and selecting the best model hyperparameters in NLP tasks is challenging due to the interplay of two major sources of variation: model sensitivity and data randomness. This variation hinders the effectiveness of the leave-one-out cross-validation method, making it necessary to employ larger fold cross validation. However, this in turn increases the variance of the model's expected performance, making it difficult to accurately predict the performance of the optimal model. This issue is particularly pronounced on limited data sets. This paper introduces an alternative, J-K fold cross validation method, which dynamically adjusts cross validation based on two main factors: model sensitivity and data size. This approach allows for balancing the bias and variance of performance estimation. Consequently, this reduction in variance enables the efficient discovery of optimal model hyperparameters even on limited data sets. This is particularly demonstrated through a series of experiments conducted on three well known NLP datasets.

Intelligent agents known as pupils are being trained to participate in challenging knowledge acquisition tasks by a class of intelligent instructors employing various teaching methods. Because neutral agents may take part in tasks without any cultural or national bias, this field draws parallels to neutral instruction. Because learning dynamics are similar to those in neutral instruction, this review focuses on knowledge acquisition through interaction between a teaching approach and learning approach. It examines the underlying mechanisms of teaching and learning, assesses the current neutral instructor-pupil models, the current neutral learning approaches, the current neutral teaching methods, and concludes by discussing potential research directions and challenging issues in the field.

We introduce a compact representation of functions called Brief Functions, which efficiently facilitate exact Maximum Probability Exponentiation (MPE) and constrained optimization tasks within graphical models. Our novel BF structure significantly accelerates explicit variable elimination, thereby enabling fast exact MPE and optimized constrained optimization. Our experiments show that using Brief Functions leads to substantial time and memory gains, outperforming state-of-the-art competitors.

Researchers utilized an ultracold $^{88}$Sr gas to enhance the sensitivity of single-beam absorption spectroscopy, overcoming limitations posed by the shot-noise constraint. By studying absorption in the $4s^1 S_0 \rightarrow 4p^1 P_1$ transition and accounting for the impact of recoil effects, a $10\%$ boost was achieved in the minimum detectable absorption. Additionally, the study demonstrated that the influence of recoil could be minimized by employing light with a high intensity, allowing for the detection of signals as weak as $10^{-4}$ times the saturation value. Furthermore, modifications to the theory of absorption were derived, incorporating the consequences of recoil and providing a solution to the Schr{\"o}dinger--Lorentzian equation. These results can be applied to various ultracold gas applications.

Global shear augmentation theory provides an explanation for how turbulence is influenced in various flows with shear, depending on a critical pitch-based diameter, Sp, and a dimensionless shear rate, A. A comprehensive review of prior research reveals that, across a broad range of flows with shear, both Sp and A can be combined into a single, unified parameter - a modified Galileo number (Ga). This unified parameter serves as the primary determinant of whether shear augmentation incites transition to turbulence or not.

Recently introduced is a class of algebras known as Racah algebras, which extend the Lie algebra of $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ through use of symmetric polynomials. A subalgebra from this class, denoted as $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, is then established for $n$ greater than one. This subalgebra demonstrates a specific structure that allows it to be equivalently defined as the set of polynomial functions applying to the algebra of symmetric functions, and satisfying particular conditions. A generating set for $Z_n(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is found, along with a natural basis for the associated vector space. Furthermore, a relationship with the special case of Fock-Bargmann-Hartwig polynomials becomes apparent. Additionally, a sequence of stabilizer algebras, parameterized by natural numbers, is given, along with its associated Hilbert-Poincaré sequence.

Online search engines such as Google adjust their results to individual users account,
based on previous queries made from the same computer browser, in an attempt to present
the most relevant information. Although this practice, known as "user and device
personalization", has become the standard for online interactions, the negative effects
it may have on understanding how much information is being missed cannot be overstated.
Studies on the subject have been limited as they require participants to search for
information on a given topic then take note of all relevant information, regardless of
whether it appears in the initial search results or further scrolling. Furthermore, they
must also be unaware of their search history. Researchers conducted two separate
experiments in public settings using public computers, one involving a familiar topic
such as weather forecast and another with a less well-known subject like the theory
of anticipatory postselection, to quantify the extent of information being overlooked.
The results show that significant amounts of information on both subjects were being
overlooked and this magnitude of missed information could be much greater for topics
with less public awareness.

The promise of a teV-scale muon-ion accelerator lies in the potential to advance our understanding of quantum chromodynamics by measuring the properties of heavy mesons in the lab using high-energy muon beams and heavy ions. This facility could also provide opportunities for advancing medical treatment by developing more effective cancer therapy and offering insights into the early universe through the study of the matter that it produced. Key challenges remain in developing key components such as powerful ion accelerators and effective cancer therapy devices. Two proposed facilities, the Muon Accelerator Program at Brookhaven National Laboratory and the J-PARC Center in Japan, are exploring this possibility and have made significant progress in the fields of physics, engineering, and medicine.

A novel approach is proposed for acquiring respiratory motion-compensated, four-dimensional T2-weighted images for bodily scanning. This method combines multiple sets of images acquired in an unrestricted breathing pattern to produce a single, high-quality image set invariant to respiratory movements. A key feature of this approach is the incorporation of advanced techniques to adjust for motion caused by respiration, allowing for seamless integration with existing rapid turbo spin-echo imaging protocols. This results in a robust method for producing high-quality, motion-free 4D T2-weighted images for various applications.

The paired-permutation test statistic (PPTS) has gained acceptance in recent years for comparing email clients in terms of usability, and our study refines this method by integrating simultaneous assessment of multiple participants and consistency of test results. Additionally, we developed a precise paired-permutation procedure for testing equality of two distributions based on permutation invariants, which encompasses the paired-permutation hypothesis for both single and multi-criteria assessments. This approach has been applied to examine permutation-based test criteria such as the structured alternative form (SAF) and the close-to-sorting (CTS) test, and has been utilized in further research to compare email client usability.

This paper presents a comprehensive set of freight cost, shipping volume, new ship price, used ship price, and scrap ship price data for the cargo shipping industry from 1966 to the present day. The dataset encompasses various shipping categories, including tankers, bulk carriers, general cargo ships, and container ships. The integrated dataset provides a unique opportunity for conducting in-depth analyses of shipping industry phenomena such as congestion charge, overcapacity, market crises, investment strategies, asset depreciation, and valuation of scrap values.

Inspired by the fabric of spacetime proposed by Godel and Wheeler, fabric spaces serve as a geometric framework that enables the investigation of spacetime configurations and their evolution. This study focuses on the specific scenario of quantum cosmology and employs the Hamiltonian constraint to define a Hamiltonian that drives the dynamics of geometric variables, resulting in a Fock space representation of physical states through a linear Schrödinger equation. By applying a differential representation of geometric variables, a new representation of physical states can be obtained, which allows for the analysis of physical properties in relation to geometric parameters. Consequently, this leads to an operator representation of the Hamiltonian constraint that enables the computation of spectral properties of the Hamiltonian, thereby providing insights into the Planckian regime. Furthermore, this approach facilitates the study of initial conditions and their impact on the early stages of inflation. A numerical approach is employed to investigate both theoretical and numerical results, which include the emergence of a classical regime within the quantum context, as well as the effects of discrete spacetime on primordial gravitational waves.

The recent interest in the stock market can be attributed to growing uncertainty driving risk-taking behavior, as forecasted by certain economic indicators. Modeling this behavior is complex and depends on various parameters, including macroeconomic data, sentiment analysis, and neural networks. In this paper, a novel ensemble method is proposed to forecast the standard deviation of the stock return's risk-taking component. This method integrates BERT-based sentiment analysis and GAN-based neural networks to improve performance. Specifically, a two-stage approach is used: first, the sentiment analysis is carried out to inform the sampling of training data; second, a separate network is trained using GAN, with the goal of predicting the standard deviation of the risk-taking component. Experiments using real data show that this method outperforms baseline models, including LSTM and GRU.

This research investigates the production of two Higgs bosons in future electron-positron colliders with an energy of 1 TeV, focusing on responses to beyond-Standard Model Higgs interactions. Initially, we consider the process where an initial electron-positron pair is transformed into two Higgs bosons through the exchange of heavy scalar or fermionic particles. We calculate the effective field theory cross-section for this process and analyze how it behaves under certain beyond-Standard Model scenarios, such as the addition of a singlet heavy scalar or a Dirac fermion with a certain charge. We also examine the contribution of these processes to specific beyond-Standard Model operators. Furthermore, we evaluate the potential of the ATLAS and HL-LLP detectors at 250 GeV and 300 GeV to identify the two Higgs boson production processes via specific decay channels, and to determine the sensitivity of these detectors to certain beyond-Standard Model operators. We find that at 250 GeV, the detection of the $hh \to b \bar{b} \gamma \gamma$ channel is feasible, while at 300 GeV, the $hh \to b \bar{b} b \bar{b}$ and $hh \to WW^* \phi^0$ channels become accessible.

We perform a symmetric polynomial expansion to achieve an accurate representation of a Gaussian process's likelihood function, thereby providing a non-parametric fit to a given dataset. This leads to a comprehensive framework for time series prediction, encompassing numerous well-known models as subcases. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations and real-world data analysis, demonstrating significant improvements over benchmark models.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular fluid by performing experiments with different speeds and surface roughness levels. The results show that the cylindrical solid experiences greater drag on its upper surface than on its lower surface, a phenomenon known as drag asymmetry. Our data indicate that the difference in surface drag is more pronounced at slower speeds and with a more roughened surface. Furthermore, the drag asymmetry is observed to decrease as the speed increases beyond a certain threshold, mirroring the behavior exhibited by a semi-circular solid moving through the same fluid-filled bed. Our study highlights the significance of considering the curved surface of a cylindrical solid in order to accurately explain and predict its drag experiences.

Recent experiments at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider have observed an unexpectedly large value of triangular flow relative momentum, particularly at its lowest multiplicity bin, which cannot be adequately explained by current models. Utilizing a multiphase transport model with initial state eccentricity, this study finds that Triangular Flow Radius, extracted using the relation $v_3 \propto \frac{1}{k_3 R_3}$, initially decreases with a rise in charged particle multiplicity but eventually turns upward, thus showing agreement with experimental data. Furthermore, a connection between initial state geometry and final state triality flow is demonstrated through specific examples of Au+Au collisions. It is also observed that in Cu+Cu collisions, due to the larger initial state eccentricity than expected from its geometry, $v_3$ exhibits a distinct minimum value.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in multiple areas, including uncommon decay processes of beauty mesons and charm quark interactions, which are crucial for further understanding the universe's fundamental composition. Specifically, uncommon decay modes of beauty mesons, such as leptonic Ds and Bs meson decays, as well as rare processes like electroweak penguin transitions, have been accurately measured by the ATLAS collaboration. Furthermore, uncommon c-jet decays, which emerge from the collision of protons, are also being studied by the ATLAS collaboration with the help of new 5.8 inverse femtobarns of data collected at the LHC's 13 TeV operating speed. These uncommon decays enable physicists to closely examine the universe's fundamental characteristics, including the magnitude of a specific particle interaction called the CP violation and the tiny asymmetry between matter and antimatter resulting from it, as well as the validity of the Standard Model of particle physics.

A critical aspect in discretizing partial differential equations involves maintaining the integrity of solution properties such as bounds, positivity, and shape transformation. While these schemes typically require the solution method to respect the underlying geometry, there is no standard way to implement this in the context of transient equations like the convection diffusion model. In our approach, we combine a shape-preserving Galerkin finite element approximation of diffusion equations with a second-order Euler scheme for time stepping. This allows us to incorporate a preconditioned GMRES solver, meeting strict stability criteria for each time step. Moreover, we establish the preservation of solution bounds and positivity in the numerical solution. Furthermore, our approach can be extended to higher-dimensional domains, where we employ a block-diagonal mass matrix as the preconditioner for good performance. Our method is compared favorably to existing approaches in test problems involving spatial and temporal shape-preserving considerations.

During minimally invasive surgical procedures, non-rigid volume-to-surface registration is a critical issue that arises when surgeons need to translate complex three-dimensional internal data to two-dimensional visualizations. However, traditional image-to-image alignment methods may not adequately account for the unpredictable movements of soft tissues, providing less accurate results. In response to this challenge, we present a novel approach that leverages a data-driven mechanical model combining the biomechanical properties and target regions of interest to guide non-rigid alignment. This model takes the preoperative volume and target surface as input and utilizes a finite element solver to compute the deformation, after which the output is compared to the target surface using a feature similarity metric to determine the optimal transformation. Furthermore, we integrate an adaptive parameter tuning process into the finite element solver to determine the most effective level of mesh refinement, resulting in a robust and efficient method for non-rigid volume-to-surface alignment with minimal user input. Our study includes a novel dataset comprising 20 abdominal organs with defined mechanical properties, making it suitable for research purposes. Experimental evaluations using both synthetic data and real clinical cases demonstrate the proposed method outperforms traditional image-to-image registration algorithms, providing more accurate results with low computational costs.

Learning scene flow from single views has been a challenging problem for computers, with most current solutions relying on traditional regression techniques and traditional distance metrics. Recent self-supervised approaches have made significant progress by utilizing unpaired images and calibrated distance metrics, achieving comparable results to supervised methods. However, the choice of distance metric used in these methods has been assumed to be optimal and not explored in depth. In contrast, we propose a novel framework, called Anti-Neighbor Network (ANN), that incorporates a robust distance metric as a trainable component, allowing it to adapt to specific datasets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on the DF-SF dataset and achieve state-of-the-art performance, surpassing the benchmarks achieved with traditional distance metrics by 13%. Furthermore, we explore different distance metric configurations on the SfM dataset and show that our approach is robust across various configurations, leading to accurate flow estimation without reliance on precise parameter tuning.

In recent years, there has been growing interest in using neural networks for content-based routing, especially in situations that require minimal computational resources, as seen in wireless sensor networks. Spike-based neural networks, with their 'event-driven' processing, offer significant advantages in areas where power consumption is a major concern. Introducing a novel, adaptive categorization approach using a Random Neural Network (RNN), it leverages the benefits of spike-based learning and allows for the dynamic reconfiguration of its components to suit varying data characteristics. This leads to not only precise grouping results but also optimized performance in terms of number of neurons and overall computation time. Furthermore, a proof is provided that showcases the optimal number of neurons required for accurate content categorization. Experimental evaluations using real-world data demonstrate the RNN's excellent performance, confirming the validity of this approach.

This research investigates the internal structure of spin-aligned strange quark stars within a thermal magnetic relativistic mean-field model, focusing on high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. By analyzing the energy density and pressure within a quark bag model, we calculate the quark distribution, mass, and charge density for both sigma and delta quarks at various temperatures and magnetic fields. Our results show that a spin-aligned quark star's mass limit significantly exceeds the predicted mass range for strange quark stars (approximately 1.97 solar masses) and displays a 0.01 solar mass range for different combinations of temperature and magnetic field. Furthermore, our calculations yield the compactness, specific heat capacity, magnetic pressure, and total pressure across a range of conditions, all of which affect the quark distribution and consequently the star's properties.

A key property of an ideal pairing is violated in the context of this paper - specifically, whether a pairing of edges in a cubic graph can be part of a Hamiltonian cycle determines predictability. A theorem by Tutte on hamiltonian pairings serves as the foundation for an in-depth exploration of ideal pairings, hamiltonian cycles, and a different concept called edge-tinting. A procedure for designing hamiltonian cycles and an associated edge-tinting pattern is outlined, thus providing a solution to the problem of determining if a given pairing is part of a hamiltonian cycle or not.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering rules in containerized applications. Following the Container Breakout Attack, researchers recognized the significance of controlling system calls from within containers. Although tools like seccomp-bpf and Google's eBPF provide efficient call filtering capabilities, establishing effective filters remains a complex, time-consuming process. In response, Timeloops offers an innovative solution, leveraging machine learning and profiling techniques to simplify system call filtering. The approach involves two phases: initial light-weight call filtering through a binary size equivalent to 10% of original size, and a second phase where machine learning algorithms analyze call histories to pinpoint suspicious patterns indicating potential malware. Evaluated across real-world containers, Timeloops succeeds in reducing call filtering size by up to 7 times and detects malicious activity with a precision of 95% and a recall of 90%.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are introduced using a lattice-based density estimation method. A key feature of this approach is the partial implementation of the birth model, where targets are categorized into known contexts rather than being identified in their entirety. Research shows that this filter can be combined with the lattice-based density estimation method to improve accuracy. A simulated radar example illustrates the effectiveness of the partial birth model.

This study investigates the null controllability of a nonlinear partial differential equation (PDE) featuring a degenerate diffusion process. Unlike typical hypoelliptic control PDEs, whose solutions enable full controllability through a single control input, this research focuses on the degenerate case to determine if internal controls can achieve null controllability. A key finding is that for a specific class of degenerate models, including the prototype $u_t = u^2 x_t + f(u) \partial^2x/|\partial y^2$ in $\Omega \times (0,T)$, full null controllability can be achieved with both internal and boundary controls.

In soccer, a draw can significantly benefit one team over the other in the standings, making the third period desperately crucial. Deep reinforcement learning has been successful in various applications but has limitations in dealing with delayed consequences. A common issue in soccer is the risk vs reward paradox, where a team must decide between conserving energy and taking bold action. In critical third-period scenarios, delayed reinforcement learning methods can result in suboptimal action choices, leading to undesirable outcomes. A deep reinforcement learning model was trained on a large dataset of simulated soccer matches, and our results show it can achieve draw benefits for the underdog team in the third period, with a 73% success rate in gaining a point. Additionally, compared to a standard policy, our model increases the energy conservation rate by 12% and average points gained in the third period by 25%.

Understanding subsurface structures is crucial for completing projects like oil and gas exploration, geotechnical engineering, and environmental remediation. To achieve this, researchers use seismic imaging techniques, particularly waveform inversion methods. These methods produce high-resolution images of the subsurface by reversing the waveform propagation process, but conventional full-waveform inversion is computationally expensive due to its large memory requirements and time-consuming nature. In contrast, surface-only seismic data and limited-aperture seismic data simplify the imaging problem, but may result in poorly resolved images. To address this, a new approach called expanded source waveform inversion was proposed, which employs multiple sources with varying locations to gather comprehensive data on the seismic medium. This information is then combined to produce a high-resolution image of the subsurface. This research paper explores time-domain expanded source waveform inversion, a new method that leverages the advantages of source expansion and generates high-resolution images of the subsurface. In time-domain, the wave equation is used to simulate seismic data, and the expanded data is combined using a weighted average. This process is achieved through a series of simulations using synthetic data, demonstrating the effectiveness of this new method in producing high-quality subsurface images.

This study examines the species coexistence, competition, and elimination dynamics in a model that combines elements of invasion size and patch dynamics, where species compete and colonize randomly in a two-dimensional torus. By utilizing an invasion size rule where species with an invasion size greater than one can invade neighboring patches, and an invasion probability proportional to their abundance in a window of nearby patches, we observe that this model exhibits a critical point at approximately $\lambda=4$ in a spatial chaos regime, diverging from the results obtained in random mixtures simulations. Additionally, the model exhibits species elimination, as well as multiple coexistence states in a one-dimensional array. We conclude that the invasion size rule can be mimicked by a Laplacian invasion size rule, which yields a continuous invasion probability. This leads to a continuous equation describing the species abundance distribution, and enables us to map the parameter space in the laboratory and "infinite garden" scenarios. Furthermore, we find that species coexistence requires that the product of the birth and death rates lies within the range $(\sqrt{\lambda}-1)^2 \leq \lambda \leq (\sqrt{\lambda}+1)^2$ for $\lambda>1$, and that the species abundance distribution follows a power law with an exponent of two for $\lambda>4$.

This paper presents an integrated surface intelligence, data, and power networking joint D2D communication framework, enabling coexistence and optimized performance in D2D networking. A key aspect of this framework is the introduction of an intellect reflecting surface that facilitates optimal D2D configuration through integrated data and power analysis. This intellect reflecting surface can be programmably designed to promote D2D performance while ensuring inter-node interference is minimized. A key challenge arises in solving an NP-hard problem, namely optimizing D2D pairing and surface configuration. To address this, a DSA-inspired scheme is proposed, leveraging a surface non-cooperative game to obtain an efficient pairing solution and a corresponding policy, while a D2D-agnostic surface configuration is derived via a heuristic algorithm, yielding near-optimal performance. Simulation results validate the efficacy of this proposed DSA-inspired scheme, demonstrating significant performance improvements over baseline random pairing and fixed surface configuration scenarios.

A flow field's precise characterization can be achieved by conducting 2D measurements using a single-point LDV system in conjunction with a control algorithm. This study investigates a control method that enables the determination of 2D velocity data from distant measurements, utilizing a spatial velocity gradient phenomenon inherent to fluid flows. This natural phenomenon serves as the foundation for developing a precise distance-based velocity estimation technique. A review of prior research reveals that previous studies primarily focused on estimating local velocity gradients rather than velocity values themselves. In contrast, this study explores the application of the Taylor series expansion to derive a precise algorithm for estimating velocity data from distant measurements. The effectiveness of this technique is validated through numerical simulations and subsequent laboratory tests using a single-point LDV system. The results demonstrate that this technique yields highly accurate 2D velocity data even from relatively distant measurements, offering practical value for various technical applications.

The problem of astigmatism in Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) images can be solved with a programmable phase disk, according to a mathematical proof presented here. The proof shows that any image acquired using a circular aperture can be precisely focused using a phase disk, regardless of the degree of astigmatism. In fact, the appropriate phase disk can be identified simply by taking two images with the same specimen but different orientations relative to the electron beam. The proposed method is validated through a simulation involving a spheroid particle and a real-world example featuring gold nanocrystals. The simplicity and effectiveness of this approach make it particularly suitable for the modern direct electron imaging applications that often involve wide-field diffraction patterns and acute electron beam incidence angles.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that combines Schrödinger and Klein-Gordon equations, and investigate these properties for a specific anharmonic operator.

We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific types of non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where G acts semi-faithfully on A, we determine that the associated rank within Gl_3(Q) is divisible by 3 if and only if there exists a subgroup of index 3 within G that acts trivially on A. Additionally, for a dihedral extension K/Q with a discriminant antenna of finite degree, we find that the rank of the Galois module Gl_3(O_K) is solely divisible by 3 if and only if the conjugate symmetry sigma_3 acts as the identity on O_K.

In the Standard Model, $B$ meson decays into invisible particles are heavily restricted, which presents a challenge for the Belle II experiment in detecting certain events. To better understand the limitations and available parameter spaces for short- or long-lived axion-like particles (ALPs) that arise from $B$ meson decays, we carry out in-depth simulations of various processes involving initial and secondary photons, electrons, and muons. Our study examines the detection possibilities for invisible $B$ meson decays at the Belle II experiment and identifies suitable constraints on the ALP mass and coupling strength. For a luminosity of $50$ ab$^{-1}$, we find that the Belle II experiment can place bounds on the ALP coupling constant in the range $3.5 \times 10^{-4}$ to $10^{-10}$, which covers both short- and long-lived ALP scenarios. Our study highlights the significance of $E_n = 5.9$ GeV in identifying disappearing tracks and enhances the detection sensitivity for low-mass ALPs with diametrically opposed decay vertices. For neutral long-lived particles with a minimum momentum of $0.5$ GeV and a decay length of at least $1$ cm, we estimate the discovery potential for various processes at the Belle II experiment, which include $e^+ e^-$, $\gamma \gamma$, and gluon-gluon fusion production mechanisms, and find that the experiment can place constraints

Recent fake news spreading and manipulation incidents highlight the importance of accurately identifying when language is being manipulated for deceptive purposes. To address this challenge, researchers have explored various contextual language models to lie or deceive detection tasks, with some achieving high accuracy rates. However, concerns about model bias and the need for extensive training data have led some to question these results. In addition, the need for more nuanced understanding of these contextual models' capabilities and limitations has been identified. In an attempt to rectify this gap, our study delves into the contextual structure of BERT and RoBERTa variants through a combination of analytical and empirical approaches, revealing how these models' pre-trained components, finetuning processes, and token-level outputs influence the detection of semantically altered text. The insights gained can be used to guide the design of lie or deceive detection contexts and input formats, and the study's methodology provides a framework for future contextual language model development and evaluation.

The theory of gravitational light-like beams surrounding rotating black holes, as postulated by Physicist Amos Dar and Professor Tamar Sotani, suggests that a new class of quasars, exhibiting extremely slow spin rates, may be illuminated by axion-like particles. Assuming that the light-like beams remain stable and based on calculations for the de-spin rates, our model estimates the minimum mass of these particles, which falls within the range of $10^{-27}$eV to $10^{12}$eV, thus encompassing both axions and additional ultralight scalar fields. Furthermore, we find that only a narrow range of masses, specifically within the range of $10^{-14}$eV to $10^{-13}$eV, yield spins below $\chi \approx 0.06$ for a $10^9$ solar mass black hole. This indicates that the light-like beams can synchronize with the quasars through a gravitational analogue of the Bloch-Swezey effect. Our model also shows that the spin rates are so slow that the light-like beams must be stable and oscillatory in nature. Consequently, the theory predicts the presence of a specific category of quasars with spin rates below a particular threshold, which can be detected by astronomers through the analysis of spin rates within a particular range of masses.

A distinctive feature of neural development is the alternating proliferation of neurons and glial cells, which occurs between the S phase and the G1 phase of the cell cycle respectively. This process, known as interkinetic nuclear migration, occurs in a wave-like pattern across the cerebral cortex and other developing brains, yet the underlying drivers of its behavior remain unclear. Recent research suggests a theory that interkinetic nuclear migration could be influenced by a feedback loop between neural stem cells and the retinoic acid pathway, although the role of this pathway in regulating the cell cycle phases remains debated. In contrast, the retinoic acid pathway does influence the timing of interkinetic nuclear migration in the developing retina of zebrafish, specifically in the central region, where it shapes the pattern of retinoblasts by controlling the phase of the cell cycle. Interestingly, the distribution of retinoblasts in this area appears disordered, unlike the linear pattern observed in the peripheral region. A new model incorporating the retinoic acid pathway provides a mathematical explanation for the pattern formation in the central region, highlighting how the dissemination of the migrating nuclei can be halted through a dispersive process mediated by the feedback loop. The termination of their movement leaves the nuclei susceptible to entering the G1 phase of the cell cycle.

In various applications such as Compressive Video Restoration and Color Image Demosaicing, images are treated as having multiple sources that have undergone different transformations, facilitating separable and efficient processing. Nonetheless, the number of sources often exceeds the number of available images, posing an underdetermined problem that calls for innovative solution strategies. Leveraging sparse and low-rank representations, we propose a novel algorithm to address this issue, where the aim is to find the optimal transformation matrix that maximizes the diversity of the data sources while ensuring that the reconstructed data adheres to certain constraints. To accomplish this, we introduce an iterative method that employs a combination of sparse and low-rank constraints in a general framework, allowing for tailored applications. When applied to demosaicing, the algorithm utilizes a novel prior that encompasses both the Riemannian manifold of positive definite matrices and the Grassmann manifold of orthogonal matrices, facilitating efficient and minimum-distance reconstruction. In compressive video restoration, the proposed algorithm employs sparse and low-rank constraints, leading to a solution that conforms to the compressive sensing framework. We evaluate and compare our algorithm against state-of-the-art approaches in both applications, demonstrating its superior performance.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active liquids in their highly congested state, taking into account the variability in their composition. Contrary to previous models, our model accounts for the dimensionless ratio of the mean-squared angle between adjacent particles remaining relatively constant over time, ranging from 1 (linear arrangement) to π^2 (random arrangement). The dynamics of this system can be represented by a set of simplified equations that incorporate the angle distribution as a key factor, in addition to the standard hydrodynamic assumptions. In dimensions greater than 2, our model demonstrates that the angle distribution becomes stabilized at a random arrangement, thus not differing significantly from incompressible active-polar dynamics in its simplified form.

The significant expansion of the internet and e-commerce has heightened the significance of verifying identities for security purposes. Identity documents, being a primary source of information, have become increasingly essential for this verification process. Unfortunately, the Indonesian language's complex nature poses a significant challenge to developing an effective document extraction system. This issue can be addressed by developing a program to automatically extract identity document contents using Indonesian as the language base. This project leverages Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques to develop an Indonesian ID Document Extractor (IIDE). The developed IIDE can accurately obtain an Indonesian identity document's relevant information. The developed algorithm's efficiency was evaluated in a test on 100 Indonesian identity documents, yielding an F-score of 0.83 for the extract-merge model and an F-score of 0.83 for the text classifier, thereby demonstrating the practical applicability of IIDE.

A new method is introduced to study a quantum harmonic oscillator with its center of mass propelled by a force, utilizing path integral techniques and Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. The purpose of this research is to provide a practical alternative to traditional numerical approaches for approximating quantum expectations in propagating quantum harmonic oscillator models. The technique introduced leverages imaginary time path integral formulations and variational Monte Carlo methods to evaluate these expectations and has the advantage of offering an exact imaginary time covariance matrix. This matrix can be approximated with high accuracy using a cumulants expansion, specifically the Gaussian approximation, which provides a precise evaluation of the quantum expectations. A comparison with traditional numerical methods such as the Lanczos algorithm is presented, demonstrating the efficiency of the introduced approach for high harmonic thickness cases.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque through non-uniform heating patterns caused by solar radiation. As a consequence, there is either acceleration or deceleration of their rotation, leading to changes in their spin periods over time. The YORP mechanism is best illustrated by the triple asteroid 1999 RQ36, however, it is also observable in other asteroids, including those with nearly circular orbits. The YORP parameter, a measure of this effect's magnitude, can be determined by analyzing the precovery and postcovery rotation periods of an asteroid, especially after calculating its orbital characteristics in detail. The study focuses on three asteroids with similar characteristics: the near-Earth asteroids 1992 SK and 1999 SH and the trojan asteroid 1685 Toro. By calculating the YORP parameter for each of these asteroids and considering other influencing factors, the research aims to investigate how YORP affects their rotation states over time, with particular attention to whether the estimated YORP acceleration leads to a positive or negative change in their spin periods.

We show that any countable collection of surface homeomorphisms that shift homeomorphisms within a fixed surface genus retain a specified property, also maintains this property when composed with a generating family of homeomorphisms for a specific group, known as I\^droisien. This result holds true for homeomorphisms defined on surfaces with boundary and closed surfaces.

In this work, regular functions that map infinite sequences to executable functions are defined. Building on the foundation established by the theory of regular sets and operations, this study demonstrates the existence of a set of functions that include composition, alternative composition, and a form of Kleisli extension. Furthermore, a characterization of the set of functions that are computable through a specified operation is presented.

The dynamics of a particle moving through a fluid is determined by the friction it experiences, which is influenced by the particle's shape, surface characteristics, and the surrounding fluid. Despite the importance of this phenomenon in nature and medicine, where particles move through the human body, the scattering of fluid particles has a limited scope in comparison to solid particles. The reason behind this distinction lies in the stability of the puller type of fluid particles, which can change to the scraper type during motion, exposing their true nature. Using the method of multiple scaling, a study on the deformation of a spherical particle in an viscous fluid reveals that the transition from the puller to the scraper type can occur even when the viscosity ratio lies within a specific, previously undetected range. The discovery of this hidden category of puller particles can also influence interpretations of experiments and the development of clinical treatments.

The concept of control reachable sets has been a significant topic in control theory and is utilized to determine the effectiveness of control strategies. Recent advancements in drone, robotics, and mobile agent navigation rely heavily on these sets, which can be used to create safe operating zones, prevent collisions, and enable navigation through unknown environments. The method of calculating control reachable sets in obstacle avoidance applications typically employs a discrete-time grid representation, but this approach can be computationally expensive and may lead to safety issues due to discretization. A more efficient solution involves employing continuous-time methods, but accurate off-line calculation tools are necessary to determine reachable sets for various scenarios. The purpose of this paper is to present an alternative approach for calculating control reachable sets in real-time, which relies on a new variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulation and employs a direct differentiation method to solve the variational HJI equation. This results in an accurate and efficient solution for $\mathcal{A}$-reachable sets, also known as attainable regions, which can be applied in real-time and is suitable for various state and input constraints.

Our study confirms the existence of a distinct animacy continuum in VTC, with humans occupying a central position. We found that the distance between a entity's animacy score and the VTC axis correlates with categorization errors, indicating that animacy influences neural responses more strongly than time. Furthermore, a break point at 0.67 on the animacy scale, which is near the value reported by Haremski et al (2020), explains behavioral and neural results. Key findings are the durability of the continuum and the absence of a segment dividing humans from other animals in VTC.

We demonstrate that for a specific class of Hecke-Maass newforms at prime power frequencies, the quantum unique ergodicity property is universally applicable. Additionally, this implication is shown to extend to Landau-Siegel zeros for all zeros located within a particular spectral range.

We introduce a new Hoare logic for a quantum relational model, extending the original idea of relational Hoare logic by Navas-Durango et al. This logic can express properties that involve expected outcomes of executions, known as anticipation properties. We prove that if a program satisfies a particular anticipation property, then its expected outcome will meet a given predicate. This result has applications in validating the expected behavior of quantum games, secure multi-party computations, and other protocols.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single individual whose highly infectious nature significantly contributes to epidemic spread. This paper explores a new transmission model that takes into account super-spreader occurrences and demonstrates through mathematical and simulation analyses that even small variations in key parameters such as the super-spreader fraction and infectious period, can lead to substantial changes in major epidemic metrics including the reproduction number, epidemic duration, cumulative cases and time to peak cases.

We codify a deep exploration of codiskcyclic collections of operators within complex topological vector spaces, drawing upon Gelfand-Shilov-type areas of study. Specifically, we provide a detailed analysis of how codiskcyclic collections of operators interact with the codiskcyclicality of associated collections of operators in the context of spaces defined by distributions, analytic functions, and Gevrey functions.

This study investigates the presence of bias in inversion techniques used to calculate vector magnetic field properties from Stokes measurements in magnetically sensitive spectral lines, particularly in regions with strong magnetic field stimulation. We employed a simulated model with stipulated vector magnetic field properties to determine the corresponding spectral line measurements and subsequently apply inversion methods to derive the associated vector magnetic field properties. The resulting properties showed discrepancies compared to the initially specified values, indicating a systematic error. We calculated the mean and standard deviation of the estimated values and found a significant scatter. To illustrate this issue, we used a semi-empirical model based on the FALPreSD solar atmosphere model and a synthetic spectrum formed by combining Stokes components with a vector additive model. This model helped us determine the bias in the inversion technique and provided a means to correct the derived measurements for magnetic field strength and inclination. We calculated the corrected values for field strength and inclination and plotted them against the initial estimated values, revealing a linear relationship that allowed us to determine the mean and standard deviation of the corrected values. We then applied these corrections to previously published vector magnetic field maps and observed a mean reduction in the field strength of 154 G and a mean change in the inclination of 5.79 degrees.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, determining an optimal transformation path can be computationally expensive. An alternative approach involves generating complex-weight neural network expectations, which provide a real-valued output that can be used in importance sampling. This method allows for the estimation of averages and variances at any Monte Carlo density ratio, making it an efficient solution for sign-problem-free simulations.

Given a non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and a reduced word w, the composition σ∗(Nw) is characterized by a directed graph whose vertices represent the images of substrings of w and the edges represent extensions of these images under σ. The number of edges in this graph determines the topological entropy of σ with respect to w, denying it the name σ(χw). Moreover, the complexity of σ(χw) can be defined as the number of vertices in the mentioned graph. If σ is uniform, then σ(χw) equals χσ(w), thereby recovering known results. Additionally, applications are shown for non-erasing free monoid morphisms and uniform automata.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to boost the cross-task generalization ability of unsupervised pre-trained language models in text domains.
A novel, end-to-end, unsupervised retrieval-augmented model is presented, which leverages levenshtein editing distance to align the model's outputs with lemmatized reference outputs, facilitating learning that generalizes across tasks.
Experiments on the Quora Question Pairs dataset showcase the model's effectiveness, with a 3.1% improvement in the F1-score.
Further analysis reveals that the model lemmatizes questions effectively, demonstrating the importance of morphological adaptation in cross-task generalization.

In order to prevent overfitting in deep learning models, regularization techniques such as dropout and max-normalization are employed in conjunction with data augmentation, often in a way that depends on the number of times the model is updated. In this study, a similar framework is proposed that incorporates a variety of deep learning regularization techniques and data augmentation methods in a way that aligns with the notion of differential privacy. A novel algorithm called Differentially Private Hyperparameter Tuning (DPHT) is developed to address the challenge of finding optimal hyperparameters within a predetermined private budget. DPHT utilizes a grid search method combined with a strategy for efficiently exploring the parameter space, allowing it to discover a suitable set of hyperparameters within a specified private budget. The proposed framework and associated algorithm are demonstrated through a series of experiments applying DPHT to tune the hyperparameters of a deep learning model in a differentially private setting. The results show that the algorithm yields a 20% reduction in the optimal private cost compared to a standard grid search method.
