A detailed investigation of the irregular NG theorem has been conducted, focusing on its applications within both relativistic and nonrelativistic physics contexts. The theorem's underlying principles have been demonstrated through explicit calculations across a broad spectrum of models, including but not limited to, the simplest scalar field theory, fermion fields, both in their single-component and pair forms, both with and without symmetry breaking under time-reversal transformation. The evidence presented below illustrates the direct connection between the number of irregular NG bosons and the mode counts affected by symmetry breaking, showing that this relationship holds true across all contexts studied.

Recent studies in counterfactual reasoning highlight the value of counterfactual conversations enabled by large language models. Nonetheless, the majority of existing approaches focus primarily on individual-level modifications, neglecting the potential for phrase-level changes. This gap in research motivates our current work to develop a novel task, phrasal counterfactual extraction, where given a text, the goal is to identify alternative phrases that could be substituted to produce a counterfactual text. We introduce a framework incorporating both text classification and replacement candidate ranking to address this challenge. To evaluate this framework and consequently assess phrasal counterfactual extraction, we create a large-scale dataset comprising nearly 60,000 counterfactual text pairs by leveraging Wikipedia's inflectional forms. This dataset allows us to explore various modeling approaches and assess the quality of counterfactual text pairs produced by the model, leveraging a metric we call CF-Score. We also investigate several strong baseline models and a strategy for incorporating extensive language models in the task. Notably, our results using T5-XL achieve a CF-Score of 43 among various modeling configurations and benchmark models, providing valuable insights for building robust phrasal counterfactual extraction models.

Our investigation focused on the competitive growth of van der Waals epitaxy, distant epitaxy, and planar diffusion of Heusler alloy layers on a graphene substrate. We observed that a 1x1 npinhole superstructure formed at equilibrium temperatures between 850-900°C, depending on the Heusler alloy used. A further increase in temperature led to the formation of large grains and a lack of long-range order in the npinhole structure. Conversely, at lower temperatures, small grains with long-range order and lacking van der Waals epitaxy, emerged. A computational model revealed that the npinhole and van der Waals epitaxy could be explained by the similarity in lattice constants between the Heusler alloy and graphene, and the facilitation of npinhole formation by reducing the enthalpy of grain boundary migration.

A code is termed $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from applying a linear transformation whose matrix entry values come from the finite field $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$ and meets the error-correcting criteria of rank and null space. This study focuses on $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes with a rank of two and a specific null space, and it is shown that all codes meeting these specifications can be generated through a specific process. Furthermore, the pair of parameters that define these codes has been determined to vary within a particular range that can be articulated algebraically.

In real-world applications, classifiers are frequently employed to identify
complex data patterns across various categories. However, in many instances,
only a single, potentially inaccurate label is obtained for each sample,
due to issues such as label noise, limited label resources, or costly label
acquisition. This paper addresses the challenge of extracting reliable,
multi-label instances from individual positive labels by leveraging a weakly
supervised learning approach. A key assumption underlying this model is the
existence of a threshold, above which the number of true labels exceeding it
is proportional to the predicted label score. By parameterizing this relation,
a general framework is established to calculate the probability of each label,
allowing for a ranking mechanism to determine the multi-label instance.
Furthermore, a specific model is proposed with a parameterizable relation
defined by a linear combination of the predicted score and its square, which
performs well in modeling various label proportion relationships. To validate
this framework, the proposed model is compared against three strong baselines
in both synthetic and real-world data, demonstrating its superior performance
across various evaluation metrics.

Quantum field theory in various formulations is based on connecting graphs to scalar values. A fundamental shift in perspective, advocated for by a few researchers, suggests viewing the relationship between graphs and their associated scalar values through the lens of linear functions between vector spaces. This perspective is particularly effective in certain theoretical frameworks such as CFT where the graph scalar value relationship can be seen as a composition of linear operations, thereby providing a categorical representation. A key feature of this representation is the presence of a specific kind of structure known as a strong unitary natural transformation. Building on this foundation, we develop a 2-categorical framework that incorporates a dual object configuration. Furthermore, we establish that the relationship between graph configurations and their associated scalar values can be seen as the image of the identity transformation on the space of configurations under a specific functor that maps configurations to complex valued functions. This functor is associated with a 2-functor that maps from the 2-category of graph configurations to the 2-category of linear functions, and is characterized by the presence of a unitary natural transformation.

Theoretical models suggesting that nearby galaxies produce gamma-rays by leveraging magnetic fields to capture and convert Milky Way star light into accretion power, have been supported by data. Based on an analysis of the spectral energy distributions for 69 nearby galaxies, we are looking for evidence of this process, particularly at its highest energies. This study employed a Bayesian approach to assess current gamma-ray satellite limits and forecast future TeV-luminosity constraints that could further validate this theory.

Early detection of heart conditions such as cardiac systolic dysfunction and valve diseases may be facilitated through automated analysis of heart sounds. Research in this area often employs recorded echocardiogram sounds that are typically acquired in a medical setting with minimal background noise. However, in other situations like physical examinations outside a medical context, machine learning models may encounter more significant obstacles due to louder background noise and motion-induced sound distortion. This study aims to explore how effectively heart sound patterns may be recognized on their own, as well as in the presence of background noise and sound deformation caused by physical movement. A comparison of several techniques including convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, and transform-based models is conducted to determine their robustness in handling noisy and distorted data. The research utilizes two datasets one clean and the other noisy, comprising 54 and 45 categories of heart sounds respectively. The findings show that the clean sound dataset yields an average accuracy of 84% when using a convolutional neural network, whereas the noisy sound dataset achieves an average accuracy of 56%. The low accuracy with noisy data may have several explanations including the presence of motion-induced sound distortion that may require a more complex model to accurately predict.

The surge in wearable healthcare devices necessitates a more efficient method for training AI models using user data. One major challenge is addressing privacy concerns that prevent data sharing. Another issue arises from the diverse characteristics of individual data sets, hindering effective model generalization. This paper presents FedHealth, a innovative framework that addresses these challenges by incorporating transfer knowledge within a federated learning framework. FedHealth enables users to train a common model collaboratively while preserving privacy and addressing dataset heterogeneity. Experimental evaluations using real data from wearable devices demonstrate the superiority of FedHealth over baseline models in terms of accuracy improvement and robustness. Additionally, FedHealth shows significant scalability and model generalization performance, meeting the requirements of real-world healthcare applications.

This study bridges two streams of research: superior moment portfolio optimization methods and option-based hedging strategies. Initially, the study provides a comprehensive review of the mean-variance model's extensions, focusing on its application in hedging and portfolio risk minimization. Notably, the study distinguishes between 'full' and 'partial' variance reduction techniques, presenting illustrative examples. Subsequently, the study introduces a new option-based 'full' hedging technique, aimed at mitigating portfolio risk in a stochastic volatility environment. The study employs a simulated scenario to evaluate and compare the proposed method with existing partial hedging techniques, considering various performance metrics.

The rise of DevOps and continuous automation has generated a need for automated testing to accommodate rapid development changes.
However, the growth of cloud-native technologies and service-based programming led to an increase in client-server interactions
within applications, making testing more complicated due to multiple moving parts.
This paper introduces a theory of Application Test Double (ATD), a concept that extends the Test Double technique to handle
complex, multi-part applications by allowing for the automated simulation of responses from remote services.
This enables developers to write more efficient and targeted test cases that can easily adapt to changes in the application.
Furthermore, a prototype of an ATD tool has been developed to facilitate the automated simulation of client-server interactions
within applications, and a case study is presented to demonstrate the benefits of ATD in real-world scenarios.

This paper examines a stochastic control problem where the cost function becomes deterministic upon a specific event occurring, which can be thought of as a toggle that activates a new control strategy. By utilizing the reflected Doob's $L^1$-estimate for one-dimensional processes, we establish the existence of an optimal strategy for this problem, and further demonstrate that the associated value function is continuous and can be obtained through the solution to a system of ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Additionally, we explore a dual problem and prove that its associated dual value function is piecewise smooth with finite jumps, and satisfies a system of ODEs at its smooth points.

To explore the potential origins of mass generation beyond the Standard Model, researchers can look at how particles interact and combine during high-energy collisions. This study examines how a specific type of particle called "leptoquarks" behave in these interactions, particularly when two particular particles called "Drell-Yan" are created simultaneously during a collision. The analysis focuses on an asymmetrical scenario where one leptoquark is much more massive than the other, and it identifies two distinct patterns of interaction based on the charge of another particle called an "electron." The analysis also aims to identify the type of leptoquark duo creation that corresponds to an experimentally observed phenomenon known as "excess" in data collected during the LHC at CERN. The analysis employs a comprehensive tool called "Monte Carlo" simulations to evaluate various leptoquark characteristics and charge configurations, and it prioritizes the most likely explanations for the "excess" based on empirical evidence from the LHC. The analysis reveals that the most plausible scenarios are characterized by a specific charge configuration and a mass ratio of approximately 1.4 between the two leptoquarks, and it also provides guidelines for conducting similar analyses with future LHC data.

A new aspect of the interstellar medium's thermal balance has been uncovered through recent high-resolution observations, revealing that some molecular gas reservoirs are subthermally excited across multiple fine-structure lines of various elements and molecules. This phenomenon has been found to be prevalent in gas reservoirs associated with low-mass stars and protostars. A particular pattern of line ratios has emerged, which may serve as an indicator of the interstellar medium's condition and provide insights into the balance of grained and gas phases. Furthermore, this ratio can facilitate measurements of gas temperature at a level of precision superior to conventional methods. A particular combination of C I line ratios has been proposed as a reliable metric for this purpose, although other lines may also serve this function. The relationship between this ratio and other physical parameters of the system, including its luminosity, density, and metallicity, has been explored, revealing that gas temperature can be determined with a precision of 10-20% using this approach. However, such calculations are highly sensitive to the assumptions made about the gas's two-component structure and properties.

This paper presents a theoretical framework for a series reconstruction challenge modelled using permutations, specifically focusing on the Hamming distance metric. In this context, we consider a time-dependent series that generates permutations, and aim to recover the original series from the resulting permutations and the underlying dynamics. A key aspect of this framework involves characterizing the ideal reconstruction performance, as well as exploring various machine learning-based prediction approaches to compare their performance to the theoretical ideal.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by the merging of eccentric black hole or neutron star binaries. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these mergers, our study finds that a particular approach based on a stationary phase approximation in time-domain produces results that are virtually indistinguishable from the exact solution, at a significantly lower computational cost. At a 1% precision in signal phase, this method takes about 50 times less time to compute than the exact solution for a 10 Hz PTA, and this time cost increases only linearly with the number of data points. By utilizing this more efficient method, PTA collaborations participating in the Oumuamua-like Eccentric Binary Merger Search project may be able to analyze 10 years of data from 64 pulsars in less than 32 hours on 64 processors, at a precision in phase evolution compatible with 1 part per million over the entire frequency range of interest.

We introduce a novel velocity randomization method for modifying the initial data in Asymptotic Simplified Semidiscrete Entropy, a system that models slender thermodynamic slumps and over which we've proven a recent stability result. Unlike traditional velocity randomization, our procedure does not disrupt the system's equilibrium states or preserve the conservation of total momentum. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that this method leads to a system of balance equations with a dissipative term that aligns with a family of rarefied gas systems, and whose stability can be ensured by a suitable choice of initial data.

Our analysis highlights the significance of considering multiple mathematical models to capture the intricate dynamics of infectious disease spread, as well as the importance of account for various data sources in epidemiological analysis. By reviewing key models, we demonstrate their similar predictive potential when using comparable data sets in estimation, yet highlight the value of compartmental models in providing a clear, intuitive view of epidemic progression. Furthermore, we address criticisms that these models are 'useless' without a clear plan for intervention, arguing that they can be viewed as tools for assessing different policy scenarios, as well as providing insights into epidemic management beyond vaccination, such as the effectiveness of non-pharmaceutical interventions.

Researchers have achieved control over specific quantum states of multiple particles through coherent light forces. However, extending this control to intricate relations between particles and'molecules' made up of two or more bound together has proven challenging. A novel scenario where a state of two colliding atoms is influenced by an intense laser beam between two specific energy levels allowing a'molecule' to form from two individual atoms, provides an opportunity to explore this complexity. By utilizing quantum simulations, it has been demonstrated that a specific diatomic molecule state can be generated from two individual atoms through intense laser interference, resulting in a particle-molecule exchange where a specific spin and parity of a'molecule' forms from three interacting spins. This research indicates that both theoretical and experimental methods are feasible for achieving massive recombination, proving that even large'molecules' made up of many interacting parts can be created from nothing through intense light interference.

This paper introduces a novel DNA storage hierarchy, consisting of a primary pool and a set of reference pools, in order to manage data fragmentation and speeding up data retrieval. Additionally, an algorithm is proposed to assist in repairing hierarchy inconsistencies and updating reference pools, with the goal of balancing pool usage and minimizing retrieval time. Computational evaluations show that this approach leads to significant improvements in data storage efficiency and retrieval speed.

The increasing use of computational models in hydrological applications is necessitating faster solutions for the shallow water equations, especially during initial flood stage assessments. Traditional numerical methods, although highly accurate, are too slow for real-time predictions. In contrast, artificial neural networks can provide fast solutions, but their accuracy has been questionable. This paper investigates the possibility of a high-accuracy fast solution for the shallow water equations by employing a limited number of grid points and time steps, achieving a $10^3$ times speedup while maintaining a high degree of precision in water level predictions.

HDR photography involves capturing and merging multiple photos taken at various exposure levels to counterbalance image details lost in high-contrast environments.  This research presents a technically straightforward HDR image creation method, suitable for entry-level mobile devices without advanced image processing capabilities.  The proposed technique leverages the built-in exposure compensation features of smartphones to rapidly capture three images at different exposure levels.  A simple yet effective algorithm is then introduced to align and fuse the images using the geometric information from the photos themselves.  Results show that this approach yields HDR images on a par with those produced by advanced, manual techniques, and significantly outperforms the standard smartphone HDR capabilities.

In recent years, causal learning has gained significant traction and multiple methods have been developed to handle various causal learning tasks, including establishing causal relationships, inferring causal effects, and reconstructing causal structures. Researchers have employed both model-based and model-free approaches, leveraging various neural network architectures and contrastive learning techniques. However, the numerous options and diverse methodologies have made it challenging to navigate this field. This paper aims to provide a concise and accessible overview of the key concepts, methodologies, and evaluations in causal learning, thereby facilitating navigation for scholars new to this area of study.

This note presents a new strategy for proving the Mumford Conjecture, which is equivalent to a specific variant of the b-principle for functors that are sensitive to surface embeddings. The proposed proof plan is based on combining the Taylor-Pardon theorem with a modified version of the Birman-Caditzereichnam-Scharlemann-Taylor inequality, and is presented in its current form to stimulate further research on the Mumford Conjecture and the b-principle.

The simulation of cardiac mechanics involves solving complex biomechanical problems with multiple moving boundaries, dependent fluid dynamics, and electrophysiological interactions. These challenges prompt the development of sophisticated numerical methods, such as finite element and lattice Boltzmann techniques, to ensure accurate and efficient simulations. Nonetheless, developing suitable computational models remains a difficulty for wide-scale applications. In an attempt to alleviate this challenge, the multilevel preconditioning technique was introduced to enable the solution of cardiac mechanics problems using simple, high-order iterative solvers. This study examines the efficacy of the multilevel preconditioning technique in conjunction with the mixed-dimensionality Schur complement method. Computational simulations of a realistic left ventricular geometry are conducted to evaluate the technique's performance. The results show that the mixed-dimensional Schur complement method outperforms the single-dimensional approach in terms of computational time. Furthermore, the introduction of electromechanical coupling leads to a significant increase in the size of the linear system, rendering the solution increasingly challenging. Nonetheless, the study finds that the use of multilevel preconditioning enables the efficient solution of large systems, even on a single GPU processor.

We investigate a two-dimensional turbulent sediment transport model with a variable bed form, focusing on the scattering of sediment grains and their resulting diffusion-like behavior. A simulation is conducted where the sediment is initially confined to a small area and allowed to diffuse across the two-dimensional space. It is observed that even though the mean grain velocity is constant throughout the domain, the distribution of the grain's position varies significantly over time - exhibiting both normal and skewed distributions in different time intervals. A key finding reveals that the distribution of the grain's position can switch between normal and anomalous diffusion in an irregular pattern, dependent on the specific scenario of sediment transport. Furthermore, we identify that the irregular pattern of sediment transport scenarios can give rise to two distinct types of diffusion - normal and anomalous - as well as a combination of both, known as superdiffusion or subdiffusion. These findings can be understood by analyzing the fluctuations in the bed form's height over time, revealing that the distribution of these fluctuations align with the distribution of the grain's position. Consequently, we can conclude that the scattering of sediment grains is primarily influenced by the irregular pattern of bed form scenarios, which vary depending on the specific scenario of sediment transport.

A fundamental model has been developed to describe both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions between the modes of optical resonators, waveguides, and fibers. The developed framework is an extension of the existing scalar mode model, enabling the analysis of interaction modes in optical devices with complex structures. A mode interaction metric, calculated from the cross-spectral density, provides a comprehensive understanding of mode interactions, extending the original model to multi-parameter analyses. The generalized model can accommodate various nonlinearity scenarios and provides a solid foundation for predicting nonlinear phenomena in a wide range of optical systems.

High-speed cameras are now the norm in fluid dynamics research, enabling the rapid capture of turbulent flow dynamics. Yet, the limited resolution of these cameras hinders precise velocity field determination through particle image velocimetry, a fundamental analysis tool. To overcome this limitation, a new super-resolution technique is proposed, leveraging generative adversarial networks to restore high-resolution velocity fields from low-resolution observations across a range of chaotic flow patterns at various Reynolds numbers. Evaluating this method on simulated and actual data shows that it accurately reconstructs high-resolution velocity fields, with results from the generative adversarial network aligning closely to those obtained through direct high-resolution observations. Furthermore, this approach is comparably efficient to other nonlinear blind inversion algorithms, capable of restoring high-resolution velocity fields from low-resolution observations acquired at multiple Reynolds numbers, including in-situ measurements.

Infinite and semi-infinite reinforcement learning benchmark settings pose a 
significant challenge for evaluating and comparing reinforcement learning
algorithms due to the asymptotic nature of their performance metrics. Such
comparisons rely heavily on timely publications of limited sets of evaluation
results by prominent research groups, leading to an uneven playing field and
undue advantage to well-resourced institutions. To address this issue, we
introduce L2Explorer, a groundbreaking evaluation ecosystem that provides a
level ground for benchmark assessments among reinforcement learning
algorithms/agents/systems. This innovative framework addresses several key
concerns related to research ethics, transparency, and accountability. With
L2Explorer, we outline a new standard for evaluating and comparing reinforcement learning agents in endless environments. This standard centers on transparent research practices, rigorous testing protocols, and a commitment to continuous, public assessment results. Our goal with L2Explorer is to foster a fair and level playing field among developers of reinforcement learning agents, where research ethics, accountability, and responsible development are prioritized. We invite industry leaders, researchers, and developers to join us in making L2Explorer a universally accepted standard for evaluating and comparing reinforcement learning agents in complex, endless environments.

The dynamic nature of business processes drives the need for a flexible
monitoring approach that enables the detection of process deviations and
trigger corresponding actions. Although various methods exist for monitoring
imperative processes, there is a lack of comparable solutions for declarative
processes. This paper addresses this shortcoming by presenting a robust,
efficient approach for detecting process deviations from streamed data.
DeclProcess is a lightweight, easy-to-set-up method providing precise
declarative process instances and deviation causes. DeclProcess handles
temporal reasoning, data streams, and plug-and-play connectivity to action
enforcers. Furthermore, DeclProcess facilitates a flexible and performance-
oriented design by offering multiple reasoning modes and providing access to
precise process instances. The benefits of DeclProcess are demonstrated
through applied research, highlighting the method's potential for supporting
exploratory business processes.

This paper provides an introduction to the use of algebraic geometry in replacing parameter spaces with compact, varied structures, ensuring the existence and properties of equations and systems are maintained through this substitution. A case study involving the construction of Birkhoff's equation's parameter space is presented, starting from an algebraic definition of the equation.

The link between the maximum stellar mass of individual galaxies and their star formation rates is a well observed trend in cosmic evolution, with a marked break point at 10 to the power of 10 solar masses. To further understand this phenomenon, researchers examined the relationship between the ratio of a galaxy's bulge to total mass, its star formation rate, and its maximum stellar mass. They utilized three distinct methods to analyze the data sets, incorporating various parameters including optical, infrared, and radio emissions, all indicating a similar pattern. As the bulge-to-total mass ratio increases from nearly zero to around 0.5, a rise is observed in the ratio of the maximum stellar mass to SFR, then the ratio decreases towards its former rate. This declinecorresponds to a transition from the peak to the tail of the galaxy mass function and marks the origin of the turning point in the SFR distribution.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional tone expressed in texts using a multi-lingual framework. The study
focuses on 4 languages: French, Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese, and uses
the Twitter Sentiment140 dataset as a reference standard for sentiment
classification. A comparative analysis of various approaches is performed to
evaluate task ordering and multi-task learning for sentiment analysis. The
results show that a randomly arranged order of tasks yields the best
performance. Additionally, the study finds that multi-task learning among the
4 languages leads to improved results compared to separate, single-language
learning approaches.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics that may indicate a patient's criticality level who has been diagnosed with COVID-19. This paper introduces a novel concept called "Dyspnoea Specific X-ray Image Features (DSXIFs)" - a set of image characteristics that are potentially correlated with the severity of dyspnoea in COVID-19 patients. A statistical approach is proposed to extract high-risk patient characteristics from X-ray images by employing standard image descriptors and statistical analysis techniques. High-risk patient characteristics can be distinguished using data-driven methods, incorporating clinical information and image features. A framework for incorporating machine learning algorithms and thresholding to achieve this differentiation is presented. Furthermore, possible DSXIFs characteristics are outlined, which can be utilized for further research on this subject.

Given a global bundle X over a base space B, defined by the surjective map p possessing the property π:X×Rk+1 ~(Sk-1) = (Bs(k)) if it is equivariant under the action of Rk+1, there exists a unique bundle whose underlying map is p and whose underlying functor is FΣk+1. Conversely, any bundle with a map possessing the property π:X×Rk+1 ~(Sk-1) = (Bs(k)) for all (s, b) in S × B is equivariant under the action of Rk+1 is a global bundle.

The issue of erroneous positives in visual association detection has been a persistent challenge, causing problems for applications such as object categorization and visual navigation. Recent methods like Visual Relationship Detection and VGG16-based association detection tasks incur high rates of incorrect detections, ranging from 50% to 90%. The sources of this error are multifaceted, stemming from ambiguous query phrases, background clutter in images, and overlapping objects. In response to this difficulty, the paper introduces a novel technique called Spatial-Aggregation Visual Relationship Detection (SAVReD), which addresses the complex interrelations in images. SAVReD leverages a residual connection in its structure, enabling the incorporation of richer global context. Additionally, it employs a innovative aggregation mechanism between the grid of objects and the grid of relationships. Experiments on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset show that SAVReD performs on a par with the current state-of-the-art methods. When evaluated on the association detection task, SAVReD exhibits significant improvements over existing approaches, yielding an mAP of 24.8% which is a 5.5% gain over the next best method.

We've performed extensive gas-rich major mergers simulation on high-redshift galaxies, and have found that even minor mergers can drive the formation of massive disks with bulges. This occurs when the gas from the companion galaxy is able to smoothly combine with that of the existing galaxy, leading to an uneven distribution of star formation. As a result, we observe a peak in the occurrence of such disk-bulge formations within environments that have experienced moderate accretion, such as in groups rather than clusters. Conclusively, our simulations demonstrate that even calm star-forming regions in clusters like the one containing GN-z11 probed by deep fields, could harbor a substantial population of galaxies with formed Hubble sequence disks.

Recently discovered documents related to solar observations hint at a possible alternative explanation for proton acceleration within the sun. Prior research assumed that specific neutron-rich isotopes' absence indicated their initial production in high energy processes. However, if high energy particles were composed solely of protons, this absence would hold little significance. A re-examination of data from the NEESR array and the Superconducting Super Collider reveals that most cosmic isotope events involve light charged particles that reduce ion charge by one unit, suggesting that high isotope masses are unlikely and supporting the notion that extensive air showers are primarily initiated by neutron-free particles. A model incorporating this concept, which forms long-lived solar particles through a specific solar process, can produce masses of solar isotopes and may have implications for our understanding of solar flares.

The newly discovered spinning star KIC 9763838 features a remarkably rapid rotation period of only 1.48 days, likely the result of substantial angular momentum acquired during a close encounter with an massive planetary body. If confirmed, this scenario would be unprecedented, departing from the conventional understanding that planets displace angular momentum into the star's core through tidal interactions, leading to a slower stellar rotation. We examine various explanations for the star's rapid rotation, including the possible presence of a giant planet causing ongoing tidal heating, as well as scenarios involving unforeseen mechanisms for angular momentum transfer, potentially related to solar pulsation-driven dynamics or magnetic regulation. Further analysis of the stellar rotation profile, combined with revised estimates of the planetary mass and semi-major axis, points to one of the following possibilities: the existence of a massive, closely orbiting planet with an absorbed energy of at least $2.75 \times 10^{32}$ ergs per day; or the presence of a dense, interior planetary object with a radius of approximately 5.5 Earth radii and a composition similar to that of Saturn, or an unforeseen mechanism transferring an angular momentum of $20\mu_{\odot}$ or more to the star over millions of years.

Due to the rapid dissemination of information on social media, fake news can spread quickly, causing significant damage to society. The issue is compounded by the large amount of counterfeit news emerging during critical events. Traditional methods rely on established facts to train models, making it difficult to tackle novel events. In response, a novel approach is proposed to address the problem of counterfeit news detection on unknown topics. The network is designed to be both meta and neural, allowing it to learn a general instruction that guides the hidden patterns in standard training data, thus becoming adept at viewing new data as input. In addition, a neural process module is introduced to provide a specific instruction that is tailored to a particular instance, by drawing on the shared knowledge. The network's ability to detect news with a designated label as counterfeit is assessed, with results showing it outperforms a standard neural network and allows for a significant reduction in the required training data. The proposed method achieves top ranks in four out of five evaluation metrics across seven text-based datasets and one multimedia dataset, demonstrating its effectiveness and versatility.

This research paper examines a recurring transport equation where the underlying space is given as a locally accessible metric domain, denoted as K. The goal is to investigate the discontinuities arising in solutions to the transport equation when the space K changes over time, represented as the time-evolutionary domain (0,T) x K, while exhibiting recurrent behavior. It has been established that the solution's discontinuities are contained within a compact subset of (0,T) x K for domains with a compact interior. Furthermore, the absence of interior boundaries is guaranteed if the initial domain K has a C^2 boundary, is locally accessible, and satisfies a certain geometric property. This property is shown to result from a space with positive curvature, including hyperbolic, spherical, and Euclidean domains. Additionally, the recurrence condition can be met if the domain K is periodically updated or varies in a continuous, differentiable manner.

Recently, Golay complementary sequences have gained prominence due to their utility in maximizing signal overlap and their potential applications in sensing technologies. This paper expands on the concept by introducing Golay complementary structures with polyphase sequences, a generalization of Golay complementary pairs. Specifically, three types of Golay complementary structures comprising polyphase sequences are presented: triad, quartet, and quintet designs. These structures maintain the same cross-ambiguity properties as their binary counterparts and provide extended flexibility in binary sequence generation. A key contribution of this research involves demonstrating that quintet designs can generate five distinct binary sequence pairs, each meeting the Golay condition, in contrast to only one pair obtainable from quintet sets in binary form. Furthermore, this work offers a novel approach to creating large sets of Golay complementary sequences by employing matrix polynomial constructions. A particular example is given where a set of 16 Golay complementary sequence pairs is generated from a single quintet design.

The behavior of silicon surface hydrosilane molecules has been elucidated in the 2D valley-spin system using silicon as a base material. Due to the weak bonding between molecules and the silicon surface, their individual properties could be identified by combining precise control of the surface's quantum states and advanced scanning tunneling microscopy/spectroscopy techniques. A range of measurements including spin-polarized tunneling, charge state control, and exchange coupling have been performed on single molecules and at temperatures relevant to mesoscopic physics. The results demonstrate robust silicon-silane bond properties and validate the validity of the minimal valley model. In addition, the findings indicate that silicon-silane bonds exhibit minimal interaction with nearby silicon surface states, which is an unusual feature. The absence of surface state interaction leads to exceptional properties, including a dimerization barrier of 194 meV, extensive spin polarization in QSH state molecules, and massive enhancement (up to 200x) in exchange coupling between nearby molecules. These outcomes suggest that silicon-silane bonds could serve as ideal references for calibrating valley-spin interactions in low-dimensional systems.

Most modern complex systems consist of multiple interacting components and can be described using graph-based representations. Identifying the internal structure and dynamics of these systems is crucial, as it can provide valuable insights for developing novel architectures and improving existing ones. A new method is introduced that leverages time-series data to automate the process of determining both the geometry and functional characteristics of graph neural network architecture, thereby enabling the exploration of complex system dynamics automatically. The proposed method can be effectively utilized for both interpolation and extrapolation tasks, as validated through comprehensive experiments performed on multiple real-world datasets. These include models of energy consumption, financial networks, and navigation systems, demonstrating substantial performance gains over conventional graph neural network approaches.

We introduce a new class of discrete partitions in N parts, which we call strictly ascending partitions, denoted as SAP(N). We establish connections between SAP(N) and elementary abelian subgroups within the symmetric group S_N. Furthermore, we calculate the generating function G(x) whose coefficients representing the number of SAP(N) configurations add up to its various degrees d, are determinants of specific combinatorial matrices related to the structure constants of the symmetric group's Grothendieck ring Z(S_N) divided by its subring Z(A_n), yielding G(x) = $\prod_{d=1}^{\infty} (1-x^d)^{\frac{1}{d^2}}$.

A recent study utilizes Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to create synthetic cerebral lesions in MRI data, overcoming previous limitations associated with generating highly complex data. Existing techniques mostly focused on simplifying data generation, leaving model performance evaluation challenging. In contrast, the proposed method employs a progressive VAE to create detailed lesion replicas while facilitating efficient training. A novel loss function is introduced to circumvent the complexity of manually crafting mask-based truth data, enabling robust model generalization. Evaluation through a feature extraction task confirms the authenticity of synthesized lesions, meeting biomedicine's rigorous standards for statistical significance. The resulting model exhibits superior performance in comparison to a conventional VAE, underscoring the advantages of progressive model design.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation rules to ease these tasks. However, determining the most effective transitions to apply to reduce the size of a program graph for analysis remains a challenging computational problem. To address this, the GP 2 framework utilizes a cost-based approach, assigning a numerical cost to each transition and selecting the lowest cost transitions to apply. While this method provides flexibility and accommodates diverse analysis goals, it necessitates a comprehensive understanding of the program language and analysis objectives. In contrast, a recent advancement in the GP 2 compiler enables the automatic creation of a cost function for each analysis task, eliminating the need for prior knowledge. This improved compiler incorporates a machine learning-based component that directly produces a cost function from a set of pre-defined features related to the program and analysis, allowing the GP 2 framework to handle diverse applications with minimal configuration.

In recent years, attribute-rich images have gained significant attention in the field of computer vision, thanks to attribute-enhanced training data and contrastive learning techniques. To tackle challenges posed by large-scale attribute-rich datasets, researchers have turned to attribute-aware models that incorporate separate heads for each attribute. However, this approach leads to multiple optimization objectives, causing increased computational costs and memory requirements. This paper proposes a unifying framework that leverages a single optimization objective to efficiently handle large-scale attribute-rich datasets. The proposed framework employs a set-wise contrastive learning approach, dividing the attribute categories into distinct sub-sets to prevent category confusion. Furthermore, we introduce a strategy to dynamically adjust the attribute sub-setting for better performance. Experimentation across multiple large-scale attribute-rich datasets validates the proposed framework's effectiveness, demonstrating improved performance and enhanced efficiency.

A graph theory context for applying Harary's star number concept leads to an interesting observation about a specific class of graphs called twisted wreath graphs. Twisted wreath graphs can be constructed using specific vertex combinations and have a distinctive structure that includes two sets of vertices connected in a particular pattern. If one set of vertices forms a complete subgraph within the graph, then another set of vertices must be arranged in a cycle to create a connected component. In this study, a condition is met if a graph contains an odd number of cycle components. When applying Harary's concept to these types of graphs, we can observe a pattern of generated subgraphs called the star number. If we repeat the star number operation over and over, the resulting subgraphs will cycle through specific configurations. Among these configurations, there is one type called the twisted wreath star network. If we remove one set of vertices from the original twisted wreath graph, then the remaining component will be the twisted wreath star network. Contrary to its name, this paper proves that there is no need for the original twisted wreath graph to include a cycle component. In fact, another type of component called the bridge component is sufficient for creating the twisted wreath star network.
